beats.heading: The game in brief
beats.narration_text: The Little Flame Witch is an H-D two-D cave action game: you aim fireballs with the mouse to fight through a cold cave. The goal is to reach the bottom and defeat the great wolf that guards it. A pit or losing all your HP sends you back, and beating the great wolf will end the game.

beats.heading: GDD 1 · Design pillars
beats.narration_text: Section one, the design pillars. Your fire is the only warmth. Every failure is fair. Readable at a glance, even muted. Small witch, big threat.
beats.script_text: Section one, the design pillars. Your fire is the only warmth. Every failure is fair. Readable at a glance, even muted. Small witch, big threat.
beats.label: constructed

beats.heading: GDD 2 · Core gameplay loop
beats.narration_text: The core loop. Moment to moment, you move, jump, aim and fire, and decide whether to shoot a growling wolf early or step out of reach. In one sitting, you'll clear a level, rest at a campfire and go on to the great wolf. A short run brings you back for a cleaner one.

beats.heading: GDD 3 · Player experience goals
beats.narration_text: The player should feel small but capable when an early fireball cancels a lunge, safe at a campfire, tense when the great wolf enters, and relieved when the cave falls quiet.
beats.script_text: The player should feel small but capable when an early fireball cancels a lunge, safe at a campfire, tense when the great wolf enters, and relieved when the cave falls quiet.
beats.label: constructed

beats.heading: GDD 4 · Core mechanics
beats.narration_text: Core mechanics, built today: A and D or the arrows to run, Space to jump, with a zero point zero eight second coyote time and no double jump, and the mouse to aim and cast. A pit or zero HP shows the reason, then the level restarts. Heal and interact will come later.
beats.script_text: Core mechanics, built today: A and D or the arrows to run, Space to jump, with a 0.08-second coyote time and no double jump, and the mouse to aim and cast. A pit or zero HP shows the reason, then the level restarts. Heal and interact will come later.
beats.label: real

beats.heading: GDD 5 · Systems: the wolf and health
beats.narration_text: Systems. Each wolf is a state machine with a phase table: growl 31 ticks, lunge 22, recover 36. A hit during the growl cancels the lunge; once the dash starts, it commits. A hit on the witch costs one of five hearts, with a tint, a blink and a second of invulnerability. The boss, hazards and campfire will follow.

beats.heading: GDD 6 · Progression
beats.narration_text: Progression: no levelling and no equipment. The witch will gain one thing, the heal spell, from the chest at the end of level one, while each level adds more wolves, then spikes and a boulder, then the great wolf.

beats.heading: GDD 7 · World and environment
beats.narration_text: The world is one cold cave under a mountain, in two to three short levels: the cave mouth, deeper tunnels if there are three, and the great wolf's den. Its one rule: warmth comes only from fire, so lit places are safe.

beats.heading: GDD 8 · Narrative
beats.narration_text: The narrative will be simple: four short, skippable scenes with portraits. She goes down with the only flame she has, rests at a campfire, is told to turn back, and is let through after the fight.

beats.heading: GDD 9 · Characters
beats.narration_text: Characters: the witch, a pixel sprite in play and a generated portrait in dialogue; the grey cave wolves that growl before they lunge; and the great wolf, which so far exists only as concept art.

beats.heading: GDD 10 · Art direction
beats.narration_text: Art direction. On the left, what exists: the pixel sprites, the four-frame run cycle, the wolf's lunge rig, my Assignment 3 props and the cave lights. On the right, the planned H-D two-D look: depth of field, bloom, fog, and the fireball as a moving light.

beats.heading: GDD 12 · Feature list
beats.narration_text: The feature list. The must column: the three-D cave and camera, the core actions in three-D, wolves with the growl cancel, two levels, the boss, HP and restart, and a Windows build with a test report. The smallest playable version: one three-D room, one wolf, and my pin passing.

beats.heading: GDD 13 · Out of scope
beats.narration_text: Out of scope: no multiplayer, no save system, no levelling, equipment or shops, no web export, and none of Assignment 4's later chapters.
beats.script_text: Out of scope: no multiplayer, no save system, no levelling, equipment or shops, no web export, and none of Assignment 4's later chapters.

beats.heading: GDD 14 · Technical requirements
beats.narration_text: Technically: Godot four point seven point two with Forward+, a Windows build, and a target of 60 frames per second at ten-eighty p on my R-T-X fifty-sixty Laptop GPU, measured, not claimed. Rooms will go from grey boxes to low-poly Blender pieces, with the sprites as camera-facing billboards.
beats.script_text: Technically: Godot 4.7.2 with Forward+, a Windows build, and a target of 60 frames per second at 1080p on my RTX 5060 Laptop GPU, measured, not claimed. Rooms will go from grey boxes to low-poly Blender pieces, with the sprites as camera-facing billboards.
beats.label: constructed

beats.heading: GDD 15 · Risks
beats.narration_text: The risks. Moving the two-D game into three-D could break what already works: I'll test one room first, judged by my Assignment 7 pin, and if it fails, the two-D layer stays and the three-D becomes the backdrop. Three levels may not fit, so the plan allows two. And if the look misses sixty frames per second, the costliest effect goes first.

beats.heading: GDD 16 · Open questions
beats.narration_text: Open questions: a two-D layer or three-D bodies on a plane, two levels or three, and whether the pixel sprites read under depth of field. Each has its test: the one-room spike, the first playable level, and captures from the first room.

beats.narration_text: Now the seven questions. What it is: when it's done, a playable Windows desktop build, a zip with an exe, of a vertical slice from title screen to end screen.

beats.heading: Question 2 · Why anyone would care
beats.narration_text: Why care? It will put Octopath Traveler's H-D two-D look together with Metal Slug-style side-scrolling, with a mouse-aimed fireball. Octopath is turn-based, Metal Slug fires in fixed directions, Hollow Knight is a large cave with progression; I've played all three. This will be a short action run.

beats.heading: Question 3 · Who opens it, and the first sixty seconds
beats.narration_text: Who opens it? A hiring manager or a lead gameplay programmer; my target role is gameplay programmer. In the first sixty seconds they'll unzip it, double-click the E-X-E, see the controls on the title screen, skip the opening line with one key, and be playing within a minute.

beats.heading: Question 4 · What it proves
beats.narration_text: What will it prove? That I can build and verify gameplay systems. The evidence started in Assignment 7: I pinned the wolf every physics tick before the growl cancel; only the two scenarios with a hit during the growl changed; and thirty-eight headless test runs passed in a fresh clone.
